chapter.title: The Dependency Array
chapter.description: The three forms of the second argument and what each one means.

blocks.text: The second argument controls when the effect re-runs. React compares each dependency with its value from the previous render using `Object.is`.
Every reactive value belongs in the array
If the effect body reads a prop, a state value, or anything derived from them, it must be listed. Leaving something out gives you an effect that keeps using a stale value from an old render.
Turn on the `react-hooks/exhaustive-deps` ESLint rule and trust it. When it complains, the fix is almost never to silence it - it is to move the value, wrap it, or restructure the effect.
Objects and functions as dependencies
A new object or function is created on every render, so it never equals the previous one and the effect runs every time. Move it inside the effect, or memoise it.
An empty array is a claim
`[]` says 'nothing this effect uses will ever change'. That is true for a one-off subscription to `window`, and usually false for anything involving props.

blocks.text: Rendering must be pure: given the same props and state, a component returns the same output and changes nothing outside itself. But real applications do need to touch the outside world - subscribe to a socket, set the document title, start an animation.
`useEffect` is where that work goes. It runs **after** React has committed the render to the DOM, so the screen is already up to date when your code runs.
The order of events

items: React calls the component and gets a new element tree.
React commits the differences to the DOM.

blocks.text: `useLayoutEffect` is identical except it runs between steps 3 and 4, before the browser paints. Use it only when you must measure or adjust layout without the user seeing a flicker - it blocks painting.
What counts as an effect

items: Subscribing to something: a WebSocket, an event listener, an observer.
Fetching data when a component appears or its inputs change.
Controlling a non-React widget such as a map or a chart library.

blocks.text: Transforming data for rendering is **not** an effect. Neither is responding to a user event - that belongs in the event handler. Reaching for an effect when a plain calculation would do is the most common misuse of the hook.

next.title: Cleanup
next.description: Returning a teardown function, and why React runs it more often than you expect.

blocks.text: An effect can return a function. React calls it before running the effect again, and once more when the component unmounts. Anything the effect started must be stopped there.
A missing cleanup is a memory leak. Timers keep firing, listeners pile up on every re-render, and sockets stay open after the component is gone.
Cleanup runs between updates, not only at the end
With dependencies, the sequence on each change is: run cleanup for the old values, then run the effect with the new ones. That is what keeps the subscription pointing at the right thing.
Strict Mode runs effects twice
In development, React Strict Mode mounts each component, runs its effects, cleans them up, and runs them again. It is checking that your cleanup actually undoes the setup.

If double mounting breaks your component - duplicate requests, a doubled counter - the effect is missing cleanup. Strict Mode did not cause the bug, it revealed one that would appear in production the first time the component remounts.
Cancelling stale requests
Async work needs guarding: a slow response for an old input must not overwrite a fresh one.
